title: Using AI Personas During Design
excerpt: I use AI personas to explore design questions and surface risks. Their responses help me decide what to investigate; they are not evidence from real users.

sources.label: Persona-Library Project Context and Reference Routing

intro: I use AI personas to explore design questions. I treat them as modeled perspectives with a clear scope, not as fictional users or a panel that can validate a design.

Before I use them, I define the problem, choose the perspectives that can help, separate evidence from assumptions and decide what each persona can influence. Then I can ask about workflows, terminology, priorities, handoffs and failure states within that scope.
Their answers help me see what to investigate. They do not replace research with real users.

sections.heading: Define the problem first
body: I start with the task, desired outcome, constraints, what I know, what I still need to learn and when to stop. I choose a persona when it brings a distinct perspective to that problem.
This helps me see whether I need more research, a clearer content model, a technical answer or a decision from someone on the team.

evidence.note: Requires an explicit user/operator job, evidence status, constraints, success criteria, and the minimum relevant Persona set.
The collaboration contract says to frame the request before selecting participants and not invent a panel.

sections.heading: Give each persona a clear role
body: Each persona needs a defined area of responsibility. If the structure, terminology or task flow is still unsettled, I use a UX perspective to work through those questions. Once the structure is clear enough, a UI perspective can focus on hierarchy, interaction states, responsive behavior, accessibility and implementation.
The perspectives can work together without blending into one generic design voice. When they disagree, I can see which design responsibility each one is considering.

evidence.note: Separates Jordan's structure/task-flow responsibility from Camille's visual/interaction/responsive/accessibility responsibility.
Routes UX versus UI work conditionally and recommends the smallest relevant set.

sections.heading: Share context when the work crosses roles
body: I use shared context when several perspectives contribute to one outcome, hand work between stages or need to keep an important disagreement visible.

The record should capture the problem, evidence, contributions, decisions, blockers, quality checks and next handoff. Then I can review how the work moved forward without relying on a chat transcript.

evidence.note: Defines when and how a shared problem-context records attributable contributions, decisions, gates, artifacts, and handoffs.
Says to use shared problem-context only when shared state and attributable handoffs are genuinely needed.

sections.heading: Ask specific questions during exploration
body: Once the roles are clear, I can ask about a particular workflow: Which terms could confuse someone? What needs to stay visible on a narrow screen? What happens when they return after an interruption? What evidence would change the recommendation?
I label a modeled answer as an assumption, recommendation or unknown. I use it to find design risks and questions to validate, not to claim that users said or wanted something.

evidence.note: Synthetic-participant guidance recommends context-specific questions about workflow, tools, terminology, priorities, handoffs, and recovery while preserving assumption status.
Requires evidence status and warns that modeled perspectives are not automatic user evidence.

sections.heading: Keep useful disagreements visible
body: If two perspectives disagree about hierarchy, interaction or risk, I record the tradeoff, the evidence each one uses, who owns the decision and what would make us revisit it.
That gives the next person a clear question to explore in a prototype or evaluation. It also shows why a later design decision changed.

evidence.note: Requires consequential disagreement and contribution dispositions to remain visible with reasons.
Calls for decisions, evidence status, alternatives, traceability, and explicit unknowns.

sections.heading: Check the design before moving on
body: I still need a design I can review: does the structure support the task? Are important states covered? Does the layout work at different screen sizes? Are keyboard and focus behavior clear? What have I not tested?

Real user evidence takes priority over a modeled perspective. If I have not validated an assumption, I leave that gap visible. The personas help me decide what to ask next; they do not remove the need to ask real people.

evidence.note: Requires state, responsive, accessibility, evaluation, handoff, and built-QA gates.
Requires a concrete solution and solution-quality gate before completion.

curationNotes: Published article describes a working method derived from current Persona-Library design and collaboration contracts.
Synthetic persona responses are explicitly not framed as observed user research.
Concrete design screenshots/examples remain deferred until their associated portfolio surfaces are approved for reuse.
